## What is a neutrino? {#what-is-a-neutrino}

:::::: {.panel-tabset}

### An invisible particle

![](media/figures/solar-neutrinos.png){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 300px;" fig-alt="Neutrinos from the Sun pass straight through the Earth: about 60 billion through a square centimetre every second."}

- An elementary particle, like the electron, but without electric charge.
- Its mass is tiny. Its exact value has still not been measured.
- It takes part only in the weak interaction, so it hardly interacts with anything.
- Through your fingernail, about a square centimetre, some 60 billion neutrinos from the Sun pass every second.
- Almost all of them pass straight through the Earth. We do not notice them.

### Why not light?

- Light is absorbed by dust and gas. Light of very high energy is lost even on the cosmic microwave background.
- Cosmic rays, protons and nuclei, are charged. Magnetic fields bend them, and the direction to the source is lost.
- A neutrino flies in a straight line and escapes even from a dense source.

::: {.takeaway}
A neutrino points straight back to its source.
:::

### The price

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- A neutrino hardly interacts. So our detector hardly notices it either.
- To catch anything at all, we need a huge target: a cubic kilometre of water or ice.
- That is about a billion tonnes!
- All of humanity would fit into half of such a cube.

::: {.question}
Where do we get such a detector?
:::
:::
